In addition, the multilayer deposition process can be tuned to have the effect of smoothing roughness in the underlying substrate.<sup>121</sup> Because of the very stringent requirements for mirror-surface figure, the multilayer films must be low stress so that they do not deform the carefully polished glass substrates.

===== [p52-55] 13.2.2 Multiple-electron-beam direct-write systems (16块) =====
--[p54]-- The multi-electron-beam systems from IMS, Vistec, and MAPPER are based on concepts that circumvent some of the inherent current limitations of singlebeam-electron lithography systems. However, increased currents will heat the wafers, and the resulting thermal expansion will cause overlay errors without compensation. $$
--[p55 [表]]-- The problem is substantially more challenging with highenergy beams. In principle, these registration errors can be corrected to some degree by detailed modeling of the wafer heating, and deflecting the electron beams to compensate.

--[p53]-- To avoid excessive heating of the aperture array plate, the energy of the electrons impinging on the plate (5 keV for the IMS system) is usually significantly less than the final 50 keV of the electrons that are focused onto the wafers. The use of multiple beams provides increased separation of the electrons as they traverse the electron-optical column, relative to single-beam systems, except at the crossover points. This reduces—but does not eliminate—the stochastic beam blur.
--[p52]-- Nevertheless, the high costs of masks and the need for more flexible manufacturing have led to efforts to develop multiple-beam systems.
Several approaches have been proposed by Vistec,<sup>46</sup> IMS,<sup>47,48</sup> and MAPPER.<sup>49</sup> All of these approaches involve micromachining to produce multiple electron beams in reasonably sized systems. However, there are also some differences among the approaches taken by each company, and these are described in this section.

--[p3]-- 12.3 EUV Masks
As discussed previously, there are no high-transmission materials at EUV wavelengths, due to the limitation imposed by atomic absorption. For EUV lithography, not only must all optical elements in the lens be reflecting, so must be the mask. A typical configuration for an EUV mask blank is shown in Fig. 12.10. A multilayer reflector is deposited on the front side of a flat, glass substrate.
--[p9]-- In order to achieve ≥90% transmission, pellicle membranes must be extremely thin. For example, a pellicle with a total thickness of 53 nm, composed of polysilicon with silicon nitride capping layers on both sides, had a transmission of 86%.<sup>74</sup> Achieving durable films of such thickness over a full exposure field is not an easy task. In addition to having adequate mechanical strength, such films also need to be able to withstand substantial thermal stresses.
The reason for such stresses originates with the thinness of the pellicle film.
--[p6]-- Such heating and subsequent cooling will lead to overlay errors due to thermal expansion and contraction of the mask, so EUV masks should be fabricated on substrates with extremely low coefficients of thermal expansion (<30 ppb/K). Glass materials with such low coefficients of thermal expansion are available and have been characterized for use as EUV mask substrates.<sup>58,59</sup> Examples of such glass materials are ULE<sup>®</sup> from Corning, Inc. and Zerodur<sup>®</sup> from Schott.
--[p6]-- It is possible to minimize the consequences of off-axis illumination by using the thinnest absorbers possible. While all materials absorb EUV light, some are more absorbing than others, and this influences the choice of materials for EUV masks.
Because EUV masks are \~30% absorbing in the reflecting areas and more in the areas with absorber, these masks will heat up during exposure.
--[p9]-- 12.19, where the multilayer is etched completely away. Very little of EUV light is reflected from the glass substrate.<sup>84</sup>
--[p6]-- 12.15, mask nonflatness will result in image-placement errors. For consistency with the overlay requirements of 16-nm half-pitch logic technology, EUV masks must be flat to within 24 nm (peak to valley; see Problem 12.6),<sup>60,61</sup> unless techniques are implemented to compensate for the pattern placement errors caused by mask nonflatness.
--[p6]-- One such method, grid matching correction for thickness variation (GMC-TV), is provided by NuFlare for their beam writers.<sup>62,63</sup> Flatness of this magnitude must be maintained while the masks are in use, which means that EUV mask chucks must also be very flat, and great care must be taken to avoid particles on the back side of the masks that can lead to front-side mask nonflatness after chucking (see Fig. 12.16).<sup>64</sup>

--[p3]-- A capping layer, typically ruthenium, is deposited on the multilayer, and then the absorber is deposited on the capping layer. --[p9]-- Moreover, as will be discussed in the next section, a spectral purity filter may also become necessary when using an EUV pellicle, reducing the overall light transmission by an additional 10%. Although the use of a pellicle is expected to result in a substantial loss of productivity, serious consideration is being given to these films, as the risk for yield loss in high volume manufacturing without a pellicle is great.
--[p3 [表]]-- In addition to absorption, criteria for choosing an EUV mask absorber include low-defect deposition, inspectability, etchability, and ease of cleaning. Masks for use in EUV lithography are fabricated in ways similar to those for optical masks that were described in Chapter 8. The capping layer provides a convenient etch stop for the patterning of the absorber and provides protection of the multilayer from damage during use and cleans.
--[p8]-- Steps can result from particles or scratches on the substrate surface on which the multilayer film is deposited, and these steps can form phase defects. The extent to which such substrate defects propagate through the multilayer is dependent upon the deposition method. While some data indicate that substrate defects can be smoothed over with ion-beam deposition techniques,<sup>67</sup> depositions that lead to high reflectance and low defects typically are fairly conformal.
Phase defects can be created by extremely small particles, which may be smaller than can be detected with optical (visible or DUV) light.
--[p8]-- Indeed, defects have been detected using actinic inspection tools that could not be found with conventional visible-light defect inspection tools.<sup>68</sup> Consequently, it is necessary to inspect masks with tools that use EUV light to provide sensitivity to phase defects.<sup>69,70,71</sup> This adds further to the cost and complexity of implementing EUV lithography. The mask is one of the biggest challenges for EUV lithography, even with the advantage of reduction lenses.
--[p9]-- On product masks, chip areas are typically surrounded by a ring of opaque material, with the intent that this will block the light from one field from exposing the resist in an adjacent field. Since 2% or more of the EUV light can be reflected from areas covered by absorber, the ring around the chip area, often referred to as the black border, will need to have a more effective solution than just absorber. One such solution is illustrated in Fig.
--[p7]-- The use of electrostatic chucks in EUV exposure systems imposes requirements on the backsides of EUV masks. In a basic bipolar Coulomb electrostatic chuck, electrodes within the chuck are charged. When the backside of a substrate is electrically conducting, charges can move freely and lead to electrostatic attraction between the chuck and the substrate (Fig. 12.17). Thus, there is a requirement in SEMI Standard P38 that the backsides of EUV masks be electrically conducting.
--[p5]-- For sub-50-nm features, horizontal–vertical print biases of 3–6 nm were seen in simulations, the magnitude depending upon the absorber composition and thickness.<sup>55</sup> Image-placement shifts of 4–6 nm were also calculated.
It was noted previously (Chapter 4) for optical lithography that there are effects that result from the 3D character of masks. For EUV lithography the horizontal– vertical print bias is one such 3D effect, and there are additional ones.
--[p9]-- The absence of highly transparent materials at EUV wavelengths implies that conventional pellicles cannot be used. The transparency requirement for EUV lithography is high because light needs to pass twice through a pellicle in the reflection geometries currently implemented. The use of very thin membranes for EUV pellicles was proposed in 2003,<sup>72</sup> but creating large area (> 110 mm × 144 mm) thin-film membranes proved challenging.
--[p9]-- Although a small amount of energy is absorbed by the pellicle, there is a very small cross section of material for conducting this energy away, and, as noted above, strong convection is not available for cooling the pellicles.<sup>82</sup> Consequently, the temperature of the portion of the pellicle being irradiated during normal wafer exposures is predicted to reach temperatures of 800<sup>o</sup>C or higher, depending on film composition and the use of coatings to improve emissivity.<sup>83</sup> Since the heating is local to the area of the pellicle under exposure, substantial stresses in the pellicle can be thermally induced. Depending upon available source power, this could limit the use of specific materials for EUV pellicles.
--[p9]-- Recently, such films have been fabricated that have \~90% transmission.<sup>73</sup> Membrane materials that have been given serious consideration include polysilicon,<sup>74</sup> silicon nitride,<sup>75,76</sup> silicon carbide,<sup>77</sup>and carbon nanotubes.<sup>78–81</sup> Because the light passes twice through the pellicle, membranes with 90% single pass transmission will lead to \~20% loss of light to the wafer plane.
--[p9]-- The areas on EUV masks covered by absorber are not completely nonreflective, and the use of thinner absorbers to reduce the impact of mask 3D effects can result in reflectances of 2% or more from the mask areas intended to be nonreflective. The primary reason for this is that EUV light will transmit to a certain extent through the absorber, with some of the light reflected from the multilayer and back out of the absorber film.
--[p5]-- Even though the angle of incidence of the illumination on the mask is small (\~6 deg mean for 0.33-NA systems), it does result in differences in the imaging of features that are parallel to the plane of incidence relative to those that are perpendicular.<sup>53,54</sup> This is because features perpendicular to the plane of incidence partially shadow the incident light (Fig. 12.12).

===== [p50-52] 13.2.1 Single-beam direct-write systems (14块) =====
--[p52]-- Hence, there is a fundamental tradeoff between resolution and throughput. Attempts to neutralize the beam with ions do not eliminate the stochastic beam blurring, which results from random interactions among particles.
The time t required to expose an area A covered with a resist of sensitivity S, using a beam of current I, is given by
$$
t = { \frac { A S } { I } } .\tag{13.7}
$$
This shows the direct relationship between beam current and throughput.
--[p50]-- 13.2.1 Single-beam direct-write systems
Direct-write single-beam electron-beam writers very similar to the mask-making systems described in Chapter 7 have been developed and built for fast-turn applications and research and development. These systems are typically vectorscan and/or shaped-beam systems when throughput is the priority, while they are Gaussian-beam systems when the highest resolution is desired.
--[p52]-- Single-beam electron lithography is proven technology and provides useful capability when patterning small areas is adequate. However, there are several obstacles to achieving the throughputs required for producing integrated circuits cost effectively with a single beam, including the need for high exposures to avoid shot-noise–induced LER, beam blur, and limitations on electronics speed.
In order to achieve writing times of less than one hour per wafer, some degree of parallel imaging is required.

The amount of beam blur depends upon the electron optical design, but Eq. (13.6) shows that the blur increases with current, regardless of the design. Single columns produce beams with blur that is too great to support the resolution requirements of the 22- nm node and beyond when the beam current reaches 10 A.
--[p51]-- This leads to a fundamental tradeoff between resolution and large-current electron beams capable of supporting high throughput.<sup>40</sup> While the resulting average field can be compensated, there is stochastic scattering—the random electron–electron interactions that will tend to broaden the beam.<sup>41</sup> Beam blur is a consequence of angular divergences within the electron beam from its nominal direction within the electron column.

Throughput was very low, 18–24 h for a single 200-mm wafer, but this was nevertheless useful for early development of advanced technologies, where few wafers were needed.

===== [p56-56] 13.2.3 Cell-projection lithography (6块) =====
--[p56]-- 7.1) is a mask of the pattern to be printed. These are typically stencil masks, where holes are made in a membrane to allow electrons to be transmitted in some areas while blocked in others. With electron optics, reduction imaging is possible, avoiding the 1 problem of masks encountered in x-ray lithography. Cell projection e-beam systems usually also have conventional single-beam lithography capability for printing the nonrepetitive parts of the pattern.
--[p56]-- 13.2.3 Cell-projection lithography
Another way to circumvent the throughput problem that is a consequence of writing pixel-by-pixel is to use some type of mask. Electron optics very similar to those used for single-beam direct systems can be used by keeping the field size small (a few microns on a side) for systems that follow this approach.
--[p56]-- One such system with a 5-m  5-m field size that was commercially available, the HL-800D from Hitachi,<sup>50,51</sup> was used to make prototype high-bit-count DRAMs<sup>52</sup> before adequate optical lithography capability became available.
--[p56]-- Interconnects among logic cells will naturally remain random, and less advantage can be applied to metal layers that connect the logic cells. Nevertheless, cell-projection lithography has potential for improving the throughput of electron-beam lithography, at least to the point where the throughput becomes limited by the wafer heating discussed in the prior section.
There are opportunities for improving throughput by choosing design rules that are optimized for cell-projection lithography.<sup>54</sup>
--[p56]-- Such an approach is clearly helpful for patterning memories, where much of the circuit area consists of repeated memory cells. As design rules have moved to smaller geometries, it is now possible to fit logic cells in a field that is only a few microns on a side, so that logic circuits can be patterned using cell-projection lithography, at least through the first few metal layers.
--[p56]-- With a resolution of 100 nm, such systems with a ${ 5 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m } \times 5 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m } }$ field size on the wafer represented an increase in the “parallelism” of electron-beam lithography by a factor of 2500 over single-beam direct-write systems. More recently, Advantest has been producing systems with cell-projection (also referred to as character-projection) capability. 53

Harry J. Levinson is currently an independent consultant and Principal Lithographer of HJL Lithography. He has spent most of his career working in the field of lithography, starting at AMD. He also held positions at Sierra Semiconductor and IBM before returning to AMD in 1994.
--[p92]-- When wafer operations were spun off from AMD he moved to GLOBALFOUNDRIES and worked there until mid-2018. During the course of his career, Dr. Levinson has applied lithography to many different technologies, including bipolar memories, 64-Mb and 256-Mb DRAM development, the manufacturing of application-specific integrated circuits, thin-film heads for magnetic recording, flash memory, and advanced logic.
--[p92]-- In recognition of his contributions to SPIE, he received the Society’s 2014 Directors’ Award.
He has a B.S. in engineering from Cornell University and a Ph.D. in physics from the University of Pennsylvania. His Ph.D. thesis, titled “Resonances and Collective Effects in Photoemission,” addressed certain phenomenon involving the interactions of light and matter. For this work he received the Wayne B. Nottingham Prize in surface science.
--[p92]-- He has published numerous articles on lithographic science, on topics ranging from thinfilm optical effects and metrics for imaging, to overlay and process control, and he is the author of two books: Lithography Process Control and Principles of Lithography. He holds over 70 US patents. Dr. Levinson is an SPIE Fellow, previously chaired the SPIE Publications Committee, and served on SPIE’s Board of Directors.
--[p92]-- He was one of the first users of 5 steppers in Silicon Valley and was an early participant in 248-nm, 193-nm and EUV lithography.
Dr. Levinson served for several years as the chairman of the USA Lithography Technology Working Group that participated in the generation of the lithography chapter of the International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors.

===== [p10-14] 12.4 Sources and Illuminators (26块) =====
--[p11]-- Lithium was considered,<sup>89,90</sup> but the dominant fuel in use today in exposure tools is tin, primarily due to its potential for high conversion efficiency to EUV light at the wavelengths where Mo/Si multilayers provide good reflectivity.<sup>91,92</sup> Conversion efficiency from infrared light energy to EUV light energy as high as 4.7% have been reported.<sup>93</sup> It should be noted that Xe continues to be used in EUV light sources for metrology applications.
As can be seen in Fig.
--[p10]-- Xenon was the target material (“fuel”) most commonly used in the light sources of early EUV systems, because it produces reasonably strong EUV emissions and, being chemically inert in its electrically neutral state, does not directly generate debris that degrades the EUV optics through contamination. However, EUV light is produced primarily by the highly charged Xe<sup>+10</sup> ionic state, so EUV light sources need to generate substantial numbers of very highly charged ions.
--[p11]-- LPP EUV sources were among the first to be considered, and such a source, using Nd-YAG lasers, was used on the first full-field EUV exposure tool.<sup>96</sup> Early cost estimates for LPP sources indicated that they would be too expensive for practical use, and discharge sources were subsequently pursued.<sup>97-100</sup> A conceptual drawing of one such discharge source is shown in Fig. 12.21, and a picture of the source in operation in shown in Fig. 12.22.
--[p14]-- 12.25.<sup>104</sup> In this system, the low pressure (a few torr) of inert gas slows down particles from the plasma, as well as provides directional changes so the particles collide with the foils and get trapped. Argon, krypton, and hydrogen are relatively weak absorbers of light at a wavelength of 13.5 nm.
--[p12]-- These droplets are then hit with very high intensity pulses at a wavelength of 10.6 m from a $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ laser, thereby generating highly ionized tin atoms. Source efficiency is another important consideration. Over 250 W of collected in-band EUV power will be required to achieve cost-effective throughput for early generations of EUV lithography, and much higher powers will be required for subsequent nodes.
--[p12]-- To achieve this, $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ laser power of 20 kW and higher are being used. With laser conversion efficiencies of 10% (electricity to light), >200 kW of electrical power will be required to sustain light sources producing 250 W of collected in-band power. Such electrical consumption is high, but not inconsistent with the electricity requirements of advanced wafer fabs.
The type of optics used to collect EUV light depends upon the source type. As seen in Fig.
--[p11]-- Discharge sources involve plasmas generated between electrodes, which can be a significant engineering constraint that limits the ability to cool the electrodes and collect EUV light.
As DPP sources came into use on exposure tools, lithographers became very conscious of the low intensities that were being achieved, and LPP sources were reconsidered.
--[p14]-- Because of all of the problems associated with LPP sources—reliability, contamination, and limitations on scaling light output—there has been recent interest in free-electron lasers<sup>105</sup> as potential EUV light sources. In a free-electron laser, an intense photon beam is produced by wiggling a beam of relativistic electrons transversely in a periodic magnetic field that is produced by a device called an undulator (Fig. 12.26).
--[p14]-- Active steps must be taken, since such elements are within line of sight of the plasma, which produces the EUV photons. All of these DPP and LPP sources that use materials other than noble gases for the “fuel” currently generate debris that coat the optics and reduce mirror reflectivity.<sup>103</sup> Various methods for protecting the collection optics have been proposed, an example of which is shown in Fig.
--[p13]-- The primary reasons for filtering the light from EUV sources is to remove long-wavelength light—DUV light that can degrade imaging and infrared light that can cause lens and wafer heating.
The considerable out-of-band light produced by LPP sources has another implication. Many EUV pellicles can have reflectivity at DUV wavelengths that exceeds 60%.
--[p10]-- Laser-produced-plasma sources are conceptually quite simple: very-high-intensity pulsed-laser light is focused onto a material, which creates a plasma containing very highly charged ions (Fig. 12.20). When electrons recombine with the ions, high-energy photons are emitted.<sup>87</sup>
--[p10]-- As discussed in Chapter 11, the amount of time required to expose the resist is proportional to the resist sensitivity divided by the light intensity. As discussed in Chapter 3 and further in Sec. 12.6, good quality patterns in resist cannot be obtained with highly sensitive resists, so high power EUV light sources are necessary for achieving cost-effective exposure tool throughputs.
--[p13]-- 12.24 that Mo/Si multilayers reflect considerable amounts of light at deep ultraviolet wavelengths, and such light often is capable of exposing EUV resists. As mentioned in Chapter 5, when mercury arc lamps are used to produce light for i-line exposure systems, it is necessary to filter out nonactinic light. This is readily accomplished using mature optical-filter technology that has been developed over centuries.
--[p13]-- 12.20, the collector mirror for a LPP source involves near-normal angles of incidence and reflection. On the other hand, grazing-mirror collection optics are needed with DPP sources (Figs. 12.21 and 12.22).
Unlike lasers, which produce very intense light within a narrow bandwidth, DPP and LPP EUV sources generate considerable amounts of light at wavelengths outside of the narrow band that is of interest for EUV lithography. It can be seen in Fig.
--[p11]-- Both companies currently use high-energy, pulsed $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ lasers at a wavelength of 10.6 m to generate the laser-produced plasma from which EUV light is emitted. A “pre-pulse” is also used to convert the spherical tin droplet to a flatter shape prior to firing the main pulse from the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ laser, which improves the efficiency of conversion from infrared to EUV light.
--[p10]-- While such sources have proven to be very useful for laboratory applications, synchrotrons cannot produce a sufficient amount of light energy within a narrow bandwidth for high-volume manufacturing while still being cost effective for exposing wafers.<sup>86</sup> Consequently, more compact sources have been developed, categorized as either discharge-produced-plasma (DPP) sources or laser-producedplasma (LPP) sources.
--[p10]-- Consequently, light sources for EUV lithography represent an area of significant active research and development.
Synchrotrons were commonly used as sources of EUV light for the early exploration of EUV lithography<sup>85</sup> and are still used today for R&D and metrology.
--[p10]-- When such ions hit a solid surface, considerable sputtering can occur.<sup>88</sup>
EUV exposure tools that use Xe-based light sources still need a scheme to mitigate damage done by these highly charged xenon ions to the condenser optics. Given a need to address condenser optics damage even with the use of a noble gas, fuel materials that provide higher EUV light output than Xe have come into use.
--[p11]-- The pre-pulse can be from a $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ laser, although some advantages have been seen by using a laser with pulses of significantly shorter temporal duration than those produced by $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ <sub>2</sub> lasers.<sup>95</sup>
--[p13]-- Because mercury arc lamps produce a considerable amount of i-line emission, exposure-tool throughput is not compromised greatly even when such filters reduce the amount of light at the desired wavelength. On the other hand, EUV lithography is a maturing technology, and EUV photons are precious. Filtering out unwanted light is a double challenge for EUV illumination systems; new technology needs to be used, and filters must reduce the amount of actinic light by the smallest amount possible.
--[p14]-- While this is not significantly different from DUV reflectivity from multilayers or absorbers, it is considerably higher than will occur from the black border. As a consequence, a spectral purity filter may be required to address this problem of DUV light, resulting in a further reduction in the light intensity at the wafer plane.<sup>102</sup>
As mentioned previously, one must avoid contaminating or eroding the optical elements that are used to collect the EUV light generated by the source.
--[p12]-- Sources have since been developed using $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ lasers that appear to have lower cost of ownership than had been projected earlier for LPP sources that employed a prior generation of Nd-YAG lasers. A picture of an LPP source that uses $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ lasers is shown in Fig. 12.23. In this source, droplets of molten tin are produced, each a few tens of microns in diameter.
--[p14]-- Because of the need to accelerate electrons to relativistic speeds, free-electron lasers are large and expensive. Most concepts for deployment involve the creation of a single, very powerful beam of EUV light, which is then split and used as the light for multiple EUV exposure tools.<sup>106</sup> Much additional development is still required to demonstrate that free-electron lasers can meet high-volume-manufacturing requirements.
--[p13]-- As discussed in Chapter 5, light from excimer lasers needs to be narrowed for lithographic applications, due to chromatic aberrations in refractive lenses or, to a lesser extent, in catadioptric lenses. The motivation for filtering EUV light is quite different. EUV lenses are all reflective, so the problem of chromatic aberrations is reduced considerably. Moreover, reflections from manifold multilayer mirrors narrow the bandwidth of the actinic light (see Problem 12.8).
--[p11]-- 12.20, the collector mirror will quickly become coated with tin without some type of active mitigation. As mentioned previously, hydrogen can be used for controlling carbon contamination of EUV optics. Hydrogen can also react with tin, forming a volatile product, stannane, $\mathrm { S n H } _ { 4 . } ^ { \mathrm { \Delta \hat { } 9 4 } }$
Today, LPP sources are being developed and built by Gigaphoton and Cymer, the principal suppliers of excimer lasers for lithographic applications.
--[p10]-- 12.4 Sources and Illuminators
As discussed at the beginning of this chapter, EUV lithography must be practiced at wavelengths where there are high-reflectivity multilayer films, rather than at wavelengths for which there are elements of nature, such as atomic or molecular spectral lines with large oscillator strengths, that can be leveraged to produce intense sources of light in a narrow bandwidth.

===== [p41-47] 13.1 Proximity X-ray Lithography (26块) =====
--[p46]-- In optical lithography, there is a focus-control requirement in order to maintain good linewidth control. There is a similar requirement for gap control in x-ray lithography.<sup>20</sup> With a 15-m nominal gap, linewidth variations of 3 nm per micron of gap change were measured for 150-nm features.<sup>21</sup> This problem of linewidth variation caused by changes in the gap increases as the targeted feature size gets smaller.
--[p46]-- \mathrm { m i n i m u m } \ : \mathrm { l i n e w i d t h } = \sqrt { \frac { \lambda g } { \alpha } } ,\tag{13.3}
$$
where $g$ is the gap between the x-ray mask and the wafer, and α is a parameter that captures the contributions from the resist process. Typically, α ranges between 0.5 and 1.5. In order to achieve resolution <100 nm, gaps less than 10 m are required. Maintaining such tight gaps is not beyond current capability, but it is a nontrivial task.
--[p44]-- Synchrotron radiation is produced by moving electrons at speeds approaching the speed of light (relativistic) along a circular arc. When this is done, synchrotron radiation is emitted in a narrow range of angles in the forward direction, along a tangent to the arc and in the same plane. By the use of extremely powerful magnets, relativistic electrons are bent in an arc, causing them to emit synchrotron radiation down a beamline connected to an xray exposure tool (Fig. 13.5).
--[p42]-- For many years, x-ray sources were a problem for lithographic applications. Point sources of x rays, such as those used in medicine or dentistry, have long been available. However, such sources are far from ideal for use in lithography. This is illustrated in Fig. 13.4, which shows that there are pattern-placement effects that do not occur with a collimated source. Since $L > > r ,$ , the displacement d is given to good approximation:
$$
d = r { \frac { g } { L } } .\tag{13.1}
$$
--[p42]-- Such films deform because of stresses, and there has been extensive work to understand and control them.<sup>8,9</sup> Mask deformation is particularly problematic for x-ray lithography, because there is no reduction of the image between the mask and wafer. This 1:1 pattern transfer necessitates very tight tolerances for the masks, relative to 4:1 or 5:1 reduction printing.
--[p42]-- On the other hand, with x rays there are no lens distortions or feature-size–dependent pattern-placement errors, so a greater part of the overlay budget can be allocated to the mask in x-ray lithography.
--[p47]-- There is also no potential for a pellicle that will keep particulate defects out of the depth-of-field. On the other hand, because there are no optics, there are no lens contributions to linewidth variation and misregistration, so 1 x-ray masks need to have linewidth variations and misregistration only about one third that of 4 reticles.
--[p46]-- This simplified the x-ray lithography development effort, since much work could be done using commercially available resist materials.
Of all the challenges to x-ray lithography, one of the greatest involved the mask. Because there is no potential for image reduction, defects, linewidth variation, and misregistration are transferred from the mask to the wafer unmitigated by the reduction found in optical steppers.
--[p46]-- For features smaller than the resolution limit of immersion optical lithography, the resolution and process control capabilities of x-ray lithography were also found to be exceeded. Thus, x-ray lithography has largely been relegated to history.
Many DUV resists, such as UVIIHS,<sup>22</sup> worked quite well as x-ray resist materials. Doses ranged from 100–300 mJ/cm<sup>2</sup> with this particular chemically amplified resist.
--[p41]-- Consequently, x-ray lithography involves the use of proximity printing, where the mask is brought to within a few microns of the wafer and the x rays are passed directly through the mask and onto the wafer (Fig. 13.1). This is in contrast to optical lithography, which has the potential for projection of the image by a lens.
--[p47]-- However, since leading-edge mask-making capability is needed just to meet the requirements of 4 reticles, this tightening of requirements by a factor of three has made 1 x-ray masks virtually impossible to make. As a consequence of the mask and resolution issues, x-ray lithography programs were scaled back considerably or terminated altogether.
--[p43]-- What this shows is that the pattern shift is a function of position on the mask and depends upon the gap. For a point source, the x-ray masks need to be fabricated with adjustment for this magnification, and a stringent requirement for gap control is imposed in order to maintain good overlay.
Because of this deficiency of point x-ray sources, synchrotron radiation was often adopted for use in x-ray lithography.
--[p45]-- Synchrotron light sources are more complex and expensive than arc lamps or excimer lasers, but are not unreasonable sources of x rays for use in lithography. Because they have no moving parts, synchrotrons are very reliable.<sup>15</sup> A single storage ring can supply x-rays for several steppers, spreading the light-source cost across multiple exposure systems.
Because x-ray light sources also produce photons at long wavelengths, a filter is needed.
--[p42]-- Because the membrane area is fragile, and silicon wafers are too thin to provide stability, frames or rings were adopted for x-ray masks. The fragile silicon wafer is bonded to the ring to provide mechanical strength. An example of such a frame, the ARPA-NIST standard,<sup>12</sup> is shown in Fig. 13.3. The frame is made of Pyrex to facilitate bonding between the frame and the silicon on which the mask is fabricated.
--[p41]-- Similarly, the lithographic use of wavelengths in the x-ray portion of the electromagnetic spectrum was motivated by the idea that diffraction effects could be effectively neutralized by using photons with extremely short wavelengths. However, at x-ray wavelengths there are no known materials for making image-forming lenses or mirrors.
--[p45]-- Beryllium is transparent for wavelengths shorter than 15 Å. Beryllium windows also enable an ultrahigh vacuum to be maintained on the source side of the window, while allowing some level of atmosphere in the exposure tools. This transmission cutoff for beryllium sets a limit for the longest wavelengths used for x-ray lithography. Another limit on the range of wavelengths for x-ray lithography is set by the membrane materials used for the x-ray mask.
--[p42]-- However, thin-film masks are susceptible to vibrations when stepped or scanned, and this needs to be addressed in any x-ray exposure system.<sup>10</sup> Diamond was pursued as an x-ray-mask-membrane material because its extremely high Young’s modulus (900 GPa) reduces mask mechanical distortion.<sup>11</sup>
X-ray masks are typically made from silicon wafers. The membrane-mask area is fabricated in the center of the wafer. The mask fabrication process is outlined in Fig. 13.2.
--[p41]-- Since there are no materials that are highly transparent, x-ray masks are made on very thin membranes (thickness <2 m) comprising low-atomic-number materials, on which the circuit patterns are placed in the form of high-atomicnumber material (Fig. 13.1). A large percentage of the x rays pass through the lowatomic-number material, but the x rays are absorbed or scattered by the highatomic-number materials, thus generating pattern contrast.
Silicon carbide is a typical membrane material, and silicon nitride films were used early in the development of x-ray lithography.
--[p44]-- This directionality, intrinsic to synchrotron radiation, is useful for x-ray lithography because mirrors and lenses cannot be used to gather photons efficiently at x-ray wavelengths and direct them toward the exposure tool. Intensity is proportional to the current of electrons. The combination of collimation and intensity make synchrotrons good sources of light for x-ray lithography.
--[p46]-- For optical lithography, the minimum printable linewidth is related to the numerical aperture of the lens, the wavelength  of the light, and the resist process, through the parameter $k _ { 1 }$ :
$$
\mathrm { \ m i n i m u m { 1 i n e w i d t h } } = k _ { 1 } \frac { \lambda } { \mathrm { N A } } .\tag{13.2}
$$
For x-ray lithography there is a similar expression:<sup>19</sup>
$$
--[p42]-- Prior to wide interest in EUV lithography, there had been greater investment in x-ray lithography than any other potential successor to optical technology. There were programs at several universities, such as MIT and the University of Wisconsin, and at companies such as IBM, AT&T, and NTT. X-ray technology also received support from the United States and Japanese governments. X-ray step-and-repeat and step-and-scan systems were made available commercially.<sup>13,14</sup>
--[p41]-- Silicon carbide is a good material to use for the membrane because it has a high Young’s modulus (450 GPa), a characteristic that minimizes mechanical distortion, and it is not damaged by long exposure to x rays.<sup>1</sup> Gold<sup>2</sup> and tungsten<sup>3</sup> have been used as absorbers, but the best success has been found with compounds of Ta, such as TaN,<sup>4</sup> TaSiN<sub>x</sub>,<sup>5</sup> and $\mathrm { T a } _ { 4 } \mathrm { B } ,$ <sup>6</sup> because they are compatible with various etch and cleaning processes.<sup>7</sup>
The use of thin membranes for masks introduces a set of challenges.
--[p45]-- A compact x-ray source has been developed that produces collimated x rays, overcoming a number of problems associated with earlier point sources.<sup>16</sup> The x rays are produced initially by hitting a copper foil with high-power light from a Nd-YAG laser (1064-nm wavelength). The resulting short-wavelength spectrum is shown in Fig. 13.6. The light is then collected by arrays of fine glass polycapillary fibers, an example of which is shown in Fig. 13.7.
--[p45]-- These enable much of the light to be collected, and the capillaries also collimate the x rays. This light source has the collimation advantages of synchrotrons but is still a compact source.
Even with wavelengths between 6.7–15.0 Å, diffraction is significant for feature sizes in the range of interest, <100 nm. Gaps between the mask and wafer typical of x-ray lithography produce configurations in which Fresnel diffraction occurs.
--[p45]-- The silicon-K absorption edge occurs at a wavelength of 6.7 Å, setting this as a lower bound on the usable wavelengths when the mask membrane is silicon carbide. There has been recent work on diamond membranes, which would enable the use of shorter wavelengths for x-ray lithography, but this technology is yet unproven. Consequently, x-ray lithography involves the use of photons with wavelengths 6.7–15.0 Å.
--[p41]-- 13.1 Proximity X-ray Lithography
Optical lithography is limited by diffraction, which is most significant when objects are comparable in size to the wavelength of light. This fact of physics has driven decreases in the wavelength of light used in optical lithography.

===== [p0-3] Principles of Lithography, Fourth Edition (Harry J. Levinson)_p501-593 (21块) =====
--[p0]-- It also means that capability must be designed into exposure tools to prevent optics from becoming contaminated by the inevitable outgassing from resists. One idea for preventing the optics from becoming contaminated is to use the flow of an inert or reducing gas at a low partial pressure, between the optics and wafer (Fig. 12.9).<sup>28–30</sup> Contaminants will be carried along by the flow of the gas, greatly reducing optics contamination.
--[p1]-- Electrostatic chucks have been used extensively in other types of semiconductor equipment where the processes occur in a vacuum, and this appears to be the approach taken for EUV systems as well. Electrostatic chucks are considered further in the next section.
As discussed in Chapter 5, very small levels of optical absorption can cause lenses to heat, leading to exposure-dependent variations in focus and overlay.
--[p3]-- The remainder of this chapter will cover particular key elements of EUV lithographic technology in more detail.
--[p1]-- Masks will also absorb an appreciable amount of light energy, which could lead to expansion and contraction of masks with attendant overlay errors.<sup>38</sup> For this reason, EUV masks are fabricated from ultralow expansion materials, with coefficients of thermal expansion measured in parts-per-billion.
Temperature control in a vacuum is more difficult than in air.
--[p2]-- Because there are no sufficiently transparent materials at EUV wavelengths, there can be no windows to segregate gases and plasmas from the rest of the optical system. The same lineof-sight paths by which EUV photons travel from the point at which they are generated to the mirrors of the collection optics can also be pathways for contamination and debris.
--[p1]-- Another interesting consequence of exposing wafers in a vacuum is the need to change the method for chucking wafers and masks. In optical scanners, vacuum clamping is used nearly universally to hold wafers and reticles onto their chucks. The force for vacuum clamping is actually provided by atmospheric pressure, so some other approach for holding wafers and masks is needed in EUV exposure tools.
--[p2]-- Such plasmas do not harm any optics because the plasmas are contained, with the light being emitted from a sealed chamber through transparent windows, typically consisting of $\mathrm { C a F } _ { 2 }$ . Such windows do degrade over time and need to be replaced periodically, but they are inexpensive relative to other types of optical components.
The situation is completely different for EUV.
--[p0]-- Such contamination on mirrors can reduce lens transmission, resulting in reduced productivity. For example, if every mirror in a six-mirror lens system becomes coated with 1-nm-thick carbon layers, the transmission of the lens will be degraded by over 7% (see Problem 12.4). This imposes the requirement that all components within the vacuum chamber be constructed of ultra-high-vacuumcompatible materials.
--[p0]-- (The transmission of 13.5-nm light through 0.1 mm of air at atmospheric pressure is only \~7%.) Moreover, the vacuum must have extremely low levels of contaminating gases, because photon-induced carbon deposition on mirror and mask surfaces or surface oxidation can result from the presence of very low levels of hydrocarbons or water in the system.<sup>25–27</sup> Indeed, carbon contamination of optics was observed on early EUV exposure tools (Fig. 12.8).
--[p0]-- Some small amount of EUV light will be absorbed by the gas, estimated to be <3% for an optimized flow, because good protection is possible even with a low partial pressure of gases. If hydrogen gas is used for such a “gas curtain,” it can remove deposited carbon through the formation of volatile gases.<sup>31</sup>
The requirement for good vacuum affects other parts of EUV scanners.
--[p3]-- As described in Chapter 5, steppers use light sensors in real time to control exposure dose. Contamination of EUV light sensors will reduce the accuracy to which exposure doses can be controlled in EUV exposure tools.
--[p2]-- Since such contamination can potentially reduce the reflectivity of such mirrors substantially, the illumination systems of exposure tools must be designed with appropriate mitigation schemes.
Contamination can affect EUV light sensors that depend on the absorption of light to produce some type of electrical signal. This is because the photoelectrical properties of all solids are very sensitive to surface conditions.
--[p1]-- It is possible to construct air bearings for the stages that can be used in vacuum,<sup>32–34</sup> but magnetic bearings have obvious advantages for EUV applications.<sup>35–37</sup> Vacuum load locks are also required for moving wafers and reticles in and out of scanners efficiently, increasing system mechanical complexity, with possible consequences for reduced reliability and increased cost.

--[p1]-- The multilayer coatings on the mirrors that comprise EUV lenses are \~70% reflective, at best, and most of the light energy that is not reflected is absorbed. --[p23]-- It is these photoelectrons that appear to be responsible for subsequent radiationinduced chemical reactions.<sup>137-140</sup> This difference in radiation chemistry is significant.
A photoelectron will propagate from its point of origin and subsequently scatter, which can result in the generation of additional energetic electrons. Many of these secondary electrons also have the potential to induce chemical reactions.
--[p24]-- Secondary electrons or photons directly convert these ligands to active sites, thereby enabling two adjacent cores to bond chemically (Fig. 12.34). --[p20]-- 12.6 EUV Resists
The demands for EUV resists differ from the requirements of photoresists used at longer wavelengths in a few ways. Because EUV lithography is intended to be used to produce features and pitches beyond the capability of ArF lithography, EUV resists must be capable of very high resolution and have low line-edge roughness. There is also an enhanced need for sensitivity because of low output of EUV light sources.

===== [p60-62] 13.4 Imprint Lithography (9块) =====
--[p61]-- Also, due to the 1× nature of the template, difficulties similar to those experienced with x-ray masks might be expected. However, there are some aspects of template fabrication for imprint lithography that make them easier to produce than x-ray masks. In particular, it was necessary to fabricate x-ray masks on thin membranes, which made registration control very difficult. In contrast, imprint templates are formed on rigid glass substrates.
--[p62]-- Nevertheless, imprint lithography is used in applications which are defect tolerant, have loose or no requirements for overlay, and low levels of integration. One example of the application of imprint lithography is the generation of patterned media for magnetic storage.<sup>81,82</sup> It has also been pursued for fabricating memories, where the potential for redundancy reduces the defect requirements.<sup>76</sup>
--[p61]-- Imprint lithography has some definite advantages and disadvantages.<sup>79</sup> Because there is no high-resolution lens required, imprint patterning tools are considerably cheaper than high-performance step-and-scan exposure tools. Offsetting this advantage is significantly less throughput than typical of optical step-and-scan systems, a consequence of the mechanical nature of imprint lithography.
--[p61]-- Although it has yet to be used for high volume manufacturing of complex integrated circuits at the time that this edition was written, nanoimprint lithography has been used outside of the semiconductor industry, and it has been deployed with multiple tools in a development pilot line.<sup>76</sup> Canon produces nanoimprint tools with capability that is targeting the overlay requirements of integrated circuit manufacturing.<sup>77</sup>
--[p61]-- With this technology, extremely-high-resolution lithography has been achieved. Not only have 20-nm features been produced, but small fabrication errors in the template of just a few nanometers in size have been replicated (Fig. 13.16). This technology clearly has high-resolution capability.
--[p61]-- To create patterns on the wafer, a small puddle of liquid imprint material is dispensed on a “field” on the wafer, and the template is pressed against the liquid to “imprint” the pattern. After imprinting, the pattern is then fixed on the wafer. With SFIL, the resist material is solidified by exposure with ultraviolet light, while heat and pressure are used with the NIL version of imprint lithography. The template is then released, and the substrate can then be etched.
--[p60]-- In one form of this technology, step-and-flash imprint lithography (SFIL),<sup>74</sup> the template is formed from glass. It was also fabricated from nickel or silicon in another form of imprint lithography that was called nanoimprint lithography (NIL).<sup>75</sup> Over time, nanoimprint has become the term applied to all imprint lithography directed at the formation of features with sizes significantly smaller than 1 µm.
Imprint tools are typically step-and-repeat.
--[p61]-- Even on glass substrates, the 1× nature of the template represents a formidable challenge, and much of the effort to enable nanoimprint lithography has been focused on template fabrication. 80
Imprint lithography is a contact-patterning method. Projection optical lithography was developed as a replacement for optical-contact printing because defect levels were too high with contact printing to support high levels of integration.
--[p60]-- 13.4 Imprint Lithography
A nonprojection lithographic technology, imprint lithography, has been introduced.<sup>73</sup> Imprint lithography is essentially a micromolding process, shown schematically in Fig. 13.15. First, a template of the pattern is created. This consists of recessed areas on a piece of a hard substance that will eventually correspond to portions of the wafer where material will remain after etch.

===== [p56-59] 13.2.4 Scattering-mask electron-projection lithography (15块) =====
--[p58]-- Simulations show that the temperature increase, which occurs nonuniformly across the mask, exceeds $7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ , causing deformations of 20 nm.<sup>64</sup> Similarly, most of the energy of the 100-keV electrons used in the SCALPEL technology is deposited into the silicon wafer, causing temperature rises calculated to be several °C.<sup>65</sup> This problem of wafer heating has already been discussed in this chapter.
--[p57]-- Another potential limitation of projection-electron lithography is mask heating. To achieve adequate throughput, high currents are needed. For masks that create opaque regions by simply blocking and absorbing the electrons, the masks become hot. To overcome this problem, a very clever scheme has been proposed,<sup>61</sup> where nearly all electrons are allowed to pass through the mask.
--[p59]-- It is possible to design electron optics that minimize electron–electron interactions, but experience in this area is limited, and the extent to which electron-optical design can address the issue of beam blur remains to be seen.
In addition to the SCALPEL program originating from Bell Labs, there was another program, PREVAIL, at IBM.<sup>55</sup> PREVAIL included the essential elements of SCALPEL, a scattering mask and focal plane aperture, but incorporated IBM’s electron-optical technology.
--[p58]-- In principle, adjustments can be performed with the electron-beam optics, rather than through mechanical motion, enabling very rapid corrections. Compensation for thermal distortions needs to be accomplished through software, which is known to be the least-reliable component of semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
--[p56]-- 13.2.4 Scattering-mask electron-projection lithography
Optics have been designed for extending electron-projection lithography beyond small field sizes $( 5 \times 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { m } )$ ).<sup>55–58</sup> However, there are two significant problems with using large-area stencil masks to exploit such optics.<sup>59</sup> First, stencil masks are very fragile,<sup>60</sup> and it has proven difficult to fabricate such masks with large areas.
--[p58]-- As with the other next-generation lithography technologies discussed thus far, such as x-ray and EUV lithography, SCALPEL masks cannot be protected by pellicles from particulate contamination. It is apparent that mask-defect mitigation will be a general problem for post-optical lithography.
Throughput was another challenge for SCALPEL. Because of the very high currents involved in a large-field approach to e-beam lithography, the problem of stochastic scattering is particularly severe.
--[p57]-- This combination of a scattering mask, in conjunction with a focal plane aperture in the electron optics, has been given the name SCALPEL, the acronym for SCattering with Angular Limitation-Projection Electron-beam Lithography. The SCALPEL approach has demonstrated patterning capability. Shown in Fig. 13.12 are 80-nm contacts created using SCALPEL.<sup>63</sup>
Membrane and stencil masks are inherently thin and fragile. Most obviously, there is the potential for damage to such masks.
--[p58]-- The amount of blur that can be tolerated decreases as feature sizes shrink. As a consequence, the beam current must be reduced in order to image smaller features with a given electron-optical system.
This leads to a familiar connection between throughput and resolution: throughput decreases in order to print smaller features.
--[p57]-- Another problem associated with large-field membrane masks is distortion, a problem that was discussed in the section on x-ray lithography. An innovative solution is to break the design into 1  12-mm sections on the masks, separated by tall struts. SCALPEL masks are usually made from silicon wafers, so the strut heights equal the thickness of a standard silicon wafer (0.75 mm for SEMI-standard 200-mm-diameter wafers).
--[p57]-- Those portions of the mask corresponding to regions of the design that are supposed to be exposed on the wafer must allow electrons to penetrate with little scattering. As an alternative to stencil masks, the scattering materials are placed on a thin membrane of low-atomicnumber material, such as silicon nitride or diamond-like carbon.<sup>62</sup> Fabricating masks on a continuous membrane, rather than by use of stencils, also increases mask manufacturability and durability.
--[p58]-- While very little energy is deposited into the SCALPEL mask, the membranes, by being so thin, have very little thermal mass, and they heat appreciably during exposures even though little total energy is deposited.
--[p57]-- Instead of absorbing electrons in those portions of the mask that are supposed to correspond to unexposed areas on the wafer, the electrons are scattered by high-atomic-number materials, such as tungsten, tantalum, or other materials used for x-ray masks. At a focal plane within the electron optics is a physical aperture, through which unscattered electrons pass. However, only a very small fraction of the scattered electrons pass through the aperture (Fig. 13.11).
--[p58]-- With 4 lens reduction, the SCALPEL field size on the wafer is 0.25 mm  3.0 mm, so the thin membrane area between the struts on the mask is 1.0 mm  12.0 mm. To create a complete chip pattern on the wafer, the individual 0.25-mm  3.0-mm fields that comprise the total field need to be stitched together.
--[p59]-- PREVAIL stands for PRojection Exposure with Variable Axis Immersion Lenses. Nikon engaged with IBM to produce exposure tools based on the PREVAIL concepts,<sup>66</sup> but this program was eventually suspended.
--[p58]-- This stitching is not a trivial challenge for the SCALPEL technology, since the left half of features, written in one field, need to line up with the right half, with a tolerance that is a small fraction of the linewidth. What complicates this stitching is the heating of the mask and wafer that occurs during exposure.

13.5 For electron-beam lithography, show that a dose of at least $1 2 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { C } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ is required to maintain <5% 3 dose variation in 22 -nm × 22-nm contacts.

===== [p62-66] 13.5 Directed Self-Assembly (10块) =====
--[p65]-- This material can then be patterned with loose-pitch optical (or other type) lithography. The resulting selfassembled pattern will resemble that in Fig. 3.21, where pitch splitting is achieved. The use of an underlayer film to guide the self-assembly<sup>86</sup> is referred to as chemical epitaxy. It is also possible to use physical features, as illustrated in Fig. 13.22. Without anchoring the pattern, self-assembling materials will form random patterns, such as seen in the left side of Fig.
--[p63]-- The thermodynamics of self-assembly is also dependent on the total number N of monomers in the block copolymer, so the quantity that is usually most relevant to DSA thermodynamics is the product $\chi \cdot N .$ Self-assembly is driven by large values of $\varkappa ^ { \cdot N . }$ Tight pitches require polymers that are comprised of few monomers, so increasing values of  are needed to offset smaller values of N.<sup>84</sup> $\chi$ $N .$
--[p64]-- Phase diagrams based on $\chi \cdot N$ and component fractions have been calculated (see Fig. 13.20).<sup>85</sup>
To be useful for fabricating semiconductor devices, it is necessary to register the arrays produced by self-assembly with patterns existing on the wafer. For example, metal lines need to be on top of contacts. One way to do this is to coat the wafer with a material that attracts one of the block types.
--[p63]-- The block copolymers are dissolved in a solvent, and the materials are applied to wafers by spin coating. Following spin-coating, the polymers are typically entangled, so the films are heated to enable mobility and phase separation (Fig. 13.19).
The thermodynamics of self-assembly depends critically on the Flory– Huggins interaction parameter $\chi$ that is proportional to the difference in free energy between neighboring monomers that are similar and dissimilar.
--[p62]-- Because of the mutual immiscibility of the different blocks, polymer chains deposited on a flat surface will be driven thermodynamically to a pattern with a degree of regularity. (Fig. 13.18a) By using blocks that provide relative etch selectivity, this pattern can be transferred to the substrate (Fig. 13.18b). For example, one block may be silicon containing, while the other is purely hydrocarbon. An oxidizing plasma etch will remove the hydrocarbons while leaving silicon-containing material.
--[p62]-- A common combination involving two hydrocarbon materials is polystyrene (PS) and polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA).<sup>83</sup> Oxygen plasma etch has provided sufficiently selectivity to be used with PS-PMMA block copolymers. Alternatively, the PMMA can be removed using vacuum ultraviolet $( \lambda = 1 7 2 \mathrm { n m } )$ flood exposure and a rinse with isopropyl alcohol.
Films for self-assembly are typically applied in a manner similar to photoresist.
--[p64]-- Suppose that the block copolymer is built from two monomers, A and B. Then another key parameter for self-assembly is the fraction $f _ { A } = N _ { A } / N ,$ where $N _ { A }$ is the number of monomers of type A. When the two block copolymers are approximately equal in size, the phases will tend to separate into lines and spaces. However, when one component is substantially large than the other, cylinders will tend to be formed, which is useful for patterning holes on wafers.
--[p66]-- Defects constitute one of the biggest challenges for enabling directed selfassembly for high-volume manufacturing.<sup>89</sup> Although there has been considerable effort to reduce defects, the level of defects in DSA has never reached a level adequate for good yield in high-volume manufacturing (Fig. 13.24).
--[p65]-- 13.23. Properly directed, selfassembled films can form useful patterns.
Figure 13.22 Pitch splitting by the use of directed self-assembly and graphoepitaxy.
It is also possible to create arrays of dots or holes by using diblock copolymers that self-assemble into cylinders (see Fig. 13.20). Depending on the properties of the specific block polymers, square or hexagonal arrays can be formed. The resulting arrays are useful for creating patterns for magnetic storage, for example.<sup>88</sup>
--[p62]-- 13.5 Directed Self-Assembly
Researchers have attempted to create patterns that might be used to fabricate integrated circuits by leveraging the inherent tendency of specific molecules to assemble into regular patterns. Self-assembly is based upon the use of polymer chains comprised of linked immiscible blocks (Fig. 13.17).

===== [p59-60] 13.3 Ion-Projection Lithography (6块) =====
--[p59]-- 13.3 Ion-Projection Lithography
Ion-beam lithography is another technology that has been explored in the laboratory but has never been used for manufacturing. Ions can also be projected through stencil masks.<sup>67</sup> Because ions scatter very little in solids, they can potentially result in very high resolution.
--[p59]-- Beam energies are typically 250 keV. Another set of electrostatic lenses then reduces the size of the overall pattern 4 and focuses the ions onto the wafer surface.
Ion-projection lithography requires stencil masks;<sup>71</sup> there is no potential for a membrane-mask option, unlike with electron-projection lithography. One of the problems with stencil masks is the donut problem. Consider the mask shape shown in Fig. 13.14.
--[p60]-- Research has shown that deposition of a carbon film provides high emissivity and resistance against ion damage to enable radiative cooling of the ion-projection masks.<sup>72</sup>
--[p59]-- However, because they are much more massive than electrons (the lightest ion, ${ \mathrm { H } } ^ { + } { \mathrm { , } }$ , is approximately 2000 more massive than an electron), ions cannot be deflected at the same speed as electrons. This is a consequence of basic physics:
$$
{ \vec { F } } = m { \vec { a } } \ .\tag{12.6}
$$
A much larger force $\vec { F }$ is required to accelerate an ion than to accelerate an electron.
--[p59]-- Consequently, the deflection schemes that have been proposed for SCALPEL cannot be easily adopted for ion-beam exposures. For this reason, largefield (12.5 mm  12.5 mm) ion-projection-lithography (IPL) systems have been pursued.
A schematic of an IPL system is shown in Fig. 13.13.<sup>68</sup> Ions with a small spread in energy are produced by a recently developed ion source.<sup>69,70</sup> Electrostatic lenses are then used to produce a uniform beam of ions that covers the area of the mask.
--[p59]-- This cannot be made with a single stencil mask, as the center portion will be unsupported and will fall out. Creation of the geometry shown in Fig. 13.14 requires the use of at least two masks. While not fundamentally limiting, the need for double exposures will reduce throughput on some layers.
Because ion masks must block ions in order to generate masked patterns, there is considerable energy deposited into the masks. With ion beams, there is also the potential for sputtering of the masks.
